title: Is stage 2 trained on leaky residuals?
shows: Left: fold MAPE when the stage-2 models learn in-sample Ridge residuals (submitted) vs out-of-fold Ridge residuals (each row's residual from a Ridge fitted on the other 80% of rows). Right: the two kinds of residual for the same rows (5,000-row sample, final training set).
finding: Largest fold difference 0.003 points. The residuals are practically identical (correlation 0.99997, largest difference 0.10% of price): Ridge has 8 coefficients fitted on 15,000–47,000 rows, so it cannot memorise its own rows. (A time-blocked out-of-fold version, tried first, was worse — 1.9% on fold 1 — because holding out a whole period makes the residuals contain period-level errors, which is a different problem from leakage.) Both variants are always scored on later months.
decision: Keep the simpler in-sample residuals; document the check.

title: The time trend: what it does and how far to push it
shows: Left: CV MAPE when, after the last training date, the trend continues at k × its fitted slope (k = 0 freezes the level at the training end; k = 1 is the submitted model). Dotted line: the same model trained without any trend term. Right: fitted drift for different training windows.
finding: Two separate effects. (1) Having a trend term at all is what matters: without it MAPE is 2.64% vs 1.61%, because the model otherwise prices every month at the training-period average level instead of the latest level. (2) How far to extend it beyond the training end matters little and depends on the period: across k = 0–1.5 the mean moves only 1.57–1.71%. Extending helps in fold 3 (1.65% → 1.39%) and hurts in fold 2 (1.64% → 2.04%), where the slope was estimated from Jan–Jun only (10.8%/yr, later revised to 7.6%/yr).
decision: Keep k = 1. The mean-optimal k = 0.5 is chosen from only three folds and differs from k = 1 by a few hundredths of a point, so tuning it would be over-fitting. The December chart is shown under k = 0, 0.5 and 1 (check 6) so the reader can see the assumption.

title: The date effect: how the 0.97 is defined and whether it carries forward
shows: Step 1: regress log(rate) on load features (log distance, equipment, log weight, quote_signal, the load's market-index deviation) plus one dummy per date (304 dates, clean labels). The dummy coefficients are the per-date price levels. Step 2: regress those levels on daily log(market_index), the quarter-end ramp and a linear trend. Left: ordinary in-sample R² of step 2. Middle/right: step 2 fitted on Jan–Aug dates only, then used to predict the Sep–Oct levels.
finding: In-sample R² rises 0.48 → 0.65 → 0.97. Out of sample, the 3-term model predicts the daily price level of unseen Sep–Oct within 0.98% RMSE, vs 2.16% for carrying the last level forward and 4.93% for market index alone (which gets the weekly wiggle but not the level). R² is not used out of sample because a 2-month window has little variance, which makes R² unstable.
decision: Describe 0.97 as an in-sample, descriptive figure; use the out-of-sample error as the evidence that the structure carries forward two months. It does not prove it holds in Nov–Dec.

title: Generalisation to unseen cities
shows: For each draw, 8 random cities are chosen. The same fold-3 loads touching them are predicted by a model trained with those cities and one trained with every load touching them removed.
finding: Removing the cities raises MAPE by 0.13 points on average (range 0.08 to 0.15); MAPE stays at 1.46–1.53%. The random cities are not the 8 real unseen validation cities (those have no labels), so this tests unseen cities in general.
decision: Evidence (not proof) that predictions for the 1,447 validation loads touching new cities should be close in quality to the rest.

title: Does removing anomalous labels help?
shows: Two-stage model trained with vs without the flagged labels (detector fitted per fold on training months), scored on clean labels and on all labels.
finding: Removing them improves accuracy on normal loads AND on all loads (anomalies included): a few labels at 3–5× or 0.2–0.4× pull a log-scale model's fit away from the bulk of the data, so keeping them makes every prediction slightly worse. The all-label error stays high either way because no model can anticipate a 4× label.
decision: Exclude them from training; report both metrics.

title: December chart: sensitivity to assumptions
shows: The fixed Lexington → Fort Wayne dry-van load priced for every December day under alternative inputs. A (submitted) uses the market_index and quote_signal values supplied for those dates in validation.csv — input features only, never labels. B and C use training data only: October training rows for market_index and quote_signal, and no validation value enters any feature (inputs saved in december_scenario_inputs.csv). The last two curves vary the trend.
finding: All scenarios lie within a $41 band (~5% of the price). The training-only forecast B differs from A by -0.0% on average (largest daily gap $5), because the weekly market pattern is very regular. The trend assumption shifts the level by about 1%.
decision: Submit A: the assessment supplies these feature values for the December dates. If only the seven chart columns may be used, B is the alternative and gives nearly the same curve.
